newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia media union urges ownership inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Australia media union urges ownership inquiry.

text.p: Australia's media union on Friday called for a detailed public inquiry into media ownership laws to remove speculation that the government was doing deals with media moguls Kerry Packer and Rupert Murdoch.

"The government should support moves for a full Senate (upper house) inquiry to enable the debate over media ownership to focus on policy issues," the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance said in a statement.

Australia's Liberal-National government has conducted a private inquiry into laws restricting cross ownership of television stations and newspapers and has indicated it may ease existing limits. The government does not have a majority in the Senate and requires the support of independent politicians.
Existing laws prevent a television operator owning more than 15 percent of a major newspaper in the same market and vice versa.

Prime Minister John Howard has held discussions in recent weeks with television network owner Kerry Packer and Rupert Murdoch, the executive chairman of News Corp Ltd which is Australia's biggest circulation newspaper group. Howard said last week he was not doing deals ahead of changes to the media rules.
"Caught trying to deal with Rupert Murdoch the government is now embarking on another deal which would further concentrate the media," the alliance said.

The Sydney Morning Herald said on Friday that the government favoured changing media ownership laws to allow Packer to buy newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, provided he sold the group's national financial daily, The Australian Financial Review. Fairfax also owns the Melbourne Age and Sydney Morning Herald newspapers.
Packer, whose Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd owns the Nine television network and several magazine titles, owns 15 percent of Fairfax, the maximum allowed under current cross-media rules.
Some Fairfax papers and The Australian newspaper have variously reported that Pearson was keen on acquiring The Australian Financial Review newspaper.
Packer is the second largest shareholder in Fairfax behind Brierley Investments Ltd of New Zealand, which has 20 percent and which under foreign investment media rules cannot go beyond 25 percent.
Fairfax shares ended five cents higher at A$3.24, valuing the publisher at A$2.46 billion based on its 758.76 million shares on issue.

Media analysts expect Packer to launch a scrip based bid which would value Fairfax at about A$3.50 per share, but some have recently said this price could prove too rich for the billionaire businessman despite his passion for taking control of the historic group.
